title: Private Class Data Pattern
oneLiner: Wraps a class's internal data in a separate, immutable holder, so not even the class's own methods can accidentally mutate it later.

hero.name: The Vault
hero.catchphrase: Your data goes in once. Nobody mutates it after — not even you.
hero.power: Encapsulates a class's core state in a separate, immutable data object, protecting it from accidental mutation by the class's own methods.
hero.weakness: For a genuinely simple class, wrapping data in a separate holder object is a layer of indirection that doesn't earn its keep.
hero.origin: The Vault appeared after a `Circle` class's own `scale()` method accidentally mutated its `radius` field mid-calculation, corrupting an area computation that assumed the radius stayed constant throughout.

story.problem: `Circle`'s own methods freely read and write `this.radius` throughout the class. A refactor accidentally mutates `radius` mid-way through `area()`, silently producing a wrong result depending on call order.
story.solution: The Vault moves `radius` into a separate, immutable `CircleData` object, set once at construction. `Circle`'s methods can only read from it — none of them, not even `Circle` itself, can mutate it after creation.
story.result: It becomes structurally impossible for any method to accidentally corrupt the circle's core data mid-calculation. The bug class disappears entirely.

before: The class's own methods can freely mutate its core fields
A refactor can accidentally corrupt state mid-method
No structural guarantee of consistency between calls
after: Core data lives in a separate, immutable holder
No method — not even the class's own — can mutate it after creation
Consistency is guaranteed structurally, not by convention

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A refactored scale() method accidentally reassigns this.radius mid-calculation, corrupting area().
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: area() gives a different answer depending on whether scale() ran first. The radius is getting mutated somewhere it shouldn't be.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Vault appears holding a sealed data box, locking the radius away from every method, including the class's own.
panels.speaker: The Vault
panels.dialogue: Don't let your own methods freely rewrite your core data. Seal it in me at construction — nobody mutates it after, not even you.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: Circle holds a private, readonly CircleData object. Every method reads from it; none can write to it.
panels.speaker: The Vault
panels.dialogue: radius is set once, at construction, inside me. Every method in Circle can read it — but not one of them can change it.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: area() now returns the exact same, correct result no matter what other methods ran before it.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: That entire bug class is gone. The radius simply can't be mutated by accident anymore — the type system won't allow it.

useWhen: A class's core data should never change after construction, but ordinary field access makes accidental mutation easy.
You want a structural (compile-time) guarantee of immutability, not just a coding convention everyone has to remember.
Bugs from unexpected mid-method state changes have actually happened, or the class is complex enough to risk them.
avoidWhen: The class's fields genuinely need to change over its lifetime — this pattern is specifically for data that shouldn't mutate.
The class is trivially simple, and the extra data-holder class adds ceremony without meaningfully reducing risk.
The language already provides simple, first-class immutability (like `readonly` fields) without needing a separate wrapper object.
commonMistakes: Applying this to fields that genuinely need to change, forcing awkward 'create a new object for every tiny update' workarounds where simple mutability would be clearer.
Forgetting that the data holder itself must be truly immutable — a mutable object exposed by reference defeats the whole point.
Over-engineering trivial classes with this pattern when a couple of `readonly` fields would achieve the same safety more simply.
Confusing this with Memento — Memento captures state at a point in time for later restoration; Private Class Data protects state from mutation throughout an object's whole life.
explanation.realWorldExample: Immutable value objects in functional-leaning codebases, `readonly` record types, and classes that return a modified copy instead of mutating themselves (a common practice in state management libraries like Redux) all embody Private Class Data's core idea.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Isn't `readonly` on a field basically the same thing?

conversation.speaker: The Vault
conversation.message: For a single field, often yes. I matter more when several related fields need to be protected TOGETHER as one consistent, immutable unit — not just individually locked, but bundled and sealed as one.

conversation.speaker: The Vault
conversation.message: When your class's data is genuinely meant to change over its lifetime. I'm specifically for state that should be set once and never touched again — forcing that on mutable data just creates awkward workarounds.

codeBattle.scenario: Your `Money` class has had two separate bugs where an internal method accidentally mutated the `amount` field mid-calculation, producing wrong totals depending on which methods ran first.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Vault seals Money's core amount in an immutable data holder set once at construction, making accidental mid-method mutation structurally impossible.

quiz.question: What does Private Class Data protect against?
options: A class's own methods accidentally mutating its core internal state
Two incompatible interfaces failing to work together
A class having too many subclasses
quiz.answer: A class's own methods accidentally mutating its core internal state
quiz.explanation: The key insight is that even the class's OWN methods are restricted from mutating the sealed data, not just outside callers.

quiz.question: How is the protected data typically structured?
options: As a separate, immutable data-holder object set once at construction
As public fields with no restrictions at all
As a global variable shared across all instances
As a database row fetched on every access
quiz.answer: As a separate, immutable data-holder object set once at construction
quiz.explanation: Isolating the data in its own immutable object is what makes accidental mutation structurally impossible.

quiz.question: How does Private Class Data differ from Memento?
options: Private Class Data prevents mutation throughout an object's life; Memento captures a snapshot at a point in time for later restoration
They are the exact same pattern with different names
Memento prevents all mutation permanently; Private Class Data allows unlimited mutation
Private Class Data requires a database; Memento does not
quiz.answer: Private Class Data prevents mutation throughout an object's life; Memento captures a snapshot at a point in time for later restoration
quiz.explanation: The two solve different problems: one is about ongoing immutability, the other is about point-in-time snapshotting for undo/rollback.

quiz.question: When is Private Class Data unnecessary?
options: When the class's fields genuinely need to change over its lifetime
When bugs from accidental mid-method state mutation have actually occurred
When a structural immutability guarantee is valuable
When several related fields need to be protected together as one unit
quiz.answer: When the class's fields genuinely need to change over its lifetime
quiz.explanation: This pattern is specifically for data meant to stay fixed after construction — forcing it onto genuinely mutable data creates awkward workarounds.
